Bernard Purdie

Drummer Bernard “Pretty” Purdie was born in Elkton, Maryland on June 11, 1939. He is often billed as “the world’s most recorded drummer” and his list of associations include Aretha Franklin, Steely Dan, Dizzy Gillespie and Gato Barbieri. He has toured Europe with the Masters of Groove Trio and produced a video entitled “The Groove Master.”
He was interviewed in West Orange, New Jersey on July 30, 2003 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe and we are in West Orange, New Jersey filming for the Jazz Archive at Hamilton College. I’m very pleased to have Bernard Purdie here with me today. Thanks for driving and meeting with me.
My plasma.
You know I’ve met some versatile musicians doing this projects, but you go from Louis Armstrong to James Brown. I think that covers a lot of turf.
Yes it does, it really does.
Was there a point as a young man where you made a conscious decision to be a musician or did it just kind of evolve?
As a young man my decision to be a musician was done as a baby.
Really.
Yeah. I was actually playing drums, tin pots, my mother and father, my parents they say at three.
No kidding.

I got my toy set at six. And it was just on from there. Because my teacher happened to be the drummer for the big band in Elkton, Maryland, which is the Cecil County School System. And he was a drummer. And I wanted to be like him. But he was also a teacher. And that’s the one thing I didn’t want to be. Whoa, was I so wrong.
Really.
Yeah. He told me that I was going to be a teacher. And I told him I do not wish that on anyone.
Because you saw him in like a school system type of teacher? Or it was a private teacher? Or both?

Both, actually for me. But being a teacher, he said the same things all the time. I mean you couldn’t get around it. He said it day after day, week after week, month after month, year after year. And I said well how do you grow? I mean I don’t understand. Why would you want to be a teacher — and not listening. That was my whole thing. I always said © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
they’re not listening. Well I was wrong of course. But it’s the one time that I can really truly say that I’m sorry that I was wrong, and I can admit that I was wrong. Once.
That’s a pretty good track record.
Well that’s been my biggest problem. That’s been the biggest problem in the world for me. Coming up in the business I was never wrong. And people took that as a very bad attitude.
Like they felt you were arrogant or something?

Yeah. To one degree yes I was. But all that arrogance and stuff that I had, I really grew out of it. But the point was is that people didn’t see that. They just knew that no matter what I said I believed in everything that I said. And it was always true. The truth always hurts. But the truth is something that’s easy to come by. And it’s something that you remember for life. The things that you have to make up gets distorted. And before you know it you lose your whole thought, what was I talking about, what, wow, what did I just do? You know you go away from what the truth is and what you fabricated dies. Oh yeah. The truth is something that will always be there because it’s in your subconscious. And whether you read it, whether were involved with it or whether you were part of it, it does come out. You can recall anything. Your mind and your memory is remarkable. All you have to do is go back to it, think about it, and before you know it you’re talking about what you lived and what you’ve been part of. And it’s scary. And I mean really scary. Because there was a lot of people out there that didn’t believe all the things I had done. Because it’s easy for me to remember, to go back to, because I lived it. And boy oh boy oh boy, it has become part of the fun of writing on my book, all the good things.
I can imagine. Yeah.

The bad things you really want to forget and you really do try very hard to forget. But at the same time, they’re there. And if you don’t go through them, and doing, like the real biography and things like that, you don’t get the hurt out.

Do you think that your memory of the bad things — and I suppose the good things — are different at all from the other people that were involved? And do you need to speak to them if you’re writing a book about how those things went down?

Well let me put it to you this way. In some incidents I would say yes, you do need those kind of things. But I also found out that no, I really don’t. I don’t need to go back to ask them about what I had done, or do they remember what I did or whatever the circumstances were. Unh uh. The hurt is already there. Just remembering. But it also cleanses you when you get it out. And I do feel very good about all of the things that have happened to me. All the ups and downs that we go through that I’ve been through in the industry. It really hurt. Because I lost a lot of friends that I thought were friends and find out that they were associates. Big difference. But you don’t know this as you’re coming © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

along because you think they’re friends. And when somebody is working with you or against you, they’re not a friend. Working with you is one thing. Working against you or working for themselves is a whole nother ballgame.
The times that those people that you thought were friends turned out not to be, was it usually a money issue? Power issue? Or can you pin it down?

Well for me, I’d say 95% of the time it was a power issue. It wasn’t even the money. Money makes power. But people who have money are really not interested or worried about making more money. They are interested in the power and what it does for them. And I got hurt a few times, I mean because of the power. I really truly did. But at the same time it was a major lesson for me that brought me through the business world. Because every time something happens — good, bad or indifferent — sshew, I could grab it and hold onto it. And it makes all the difference in the world when you can go back to it and relate to it, and just make yourself better, even if it hurts you, to stop somebody else from falling into that trap.
That’s really interesting.

But I had good teachers. That makes the difference. It’s the teachers who give you the body, the instincts and things like that that you don’t have to be bitter, and you don’t have to be bad, because it happened to you. You can actually make it comfortable for somebody else. And in the long run it will make it better for you. It makes you a better person.
Who were the teachers that you would credit?
Well my biggest teacher was Leonard Heywood. That was my first teacher and he was my music teacher, my drum teacher, he was the band director for the school, and my mentor.
The last name was Haven?

Heywood. Leonard Heywood. When I lost him, he moved to — well his wife said — moved to Phoenix, Arizona, for his health. Well I have no idea if that was true or not. As far as I’m concerned it was. Because she said it. But as time and the years go by it makes you wonder. Did they split up? He was an alcoholic, but of course I didn’t know what that was. They said he had a breathing problem. Okay, Arizona was the dry place. I mean I had the whole spiel. It was all given to me. And I believed it. Totally believed it. I had never thought anything different. I had no reason to think that anything was different until 20, 30 years later, when you start asking and asking and then the things change on you. Well I just started hearing all kinds of stories. But who knows why? I was not that inquisitive to that point to want to know why they broke up, why they separated, why they divorced, whatever they did. I still have no idea. He was my mentor, he was my teacher, I loved him, and what I wanted to do was dedicate my book, my first book, and © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
anything else that I could do over the course of the years, to him. Because of what he did for me.
That’s nice.
And still it will happen, and I’ll just keep on doing it.
Did someone step in to kind of fill that void for you when he left? Another teacher?

Well actually it was more than that. Not one, not someone, but many. I ended up having many teachers because I looked at it that all my teachers in school, well not all, 90% of my teachers in school, I loved them. And they all were on my case. Now I thought that they were on my case for different reasons, until you find out that every one of them was there to help me. And they did help me. Because I could go back and relate to it, what they said, and then when other people, as the years went on would say wow man, that must have been a great lesson for you, and I went huh, oh yes, oh my God, they were helping me. I mean all of a sudden the light just shone, to how many people were helping me over the course of the years. And it was amazing. There was always somebody helping me. So I had to go back to find out why. And for me it was like you really are a nice guy. You are a pain in the neck, but you are a nice guy. And it was like okay, I can deal with this. Yes I know I’m realizing I’m a pain in the neck. But I never meant to harm anybody. I was always trying to do the job. And it was always the job first, because that’s what I was taught. You do the job, then you have your fun. But why not do your job and have fun with it? That was my motto. Why can’t I do both at the same time? And nobody said that you couldn’t. He said but you must learn to watch your mouth. You’ve got a mouth problem. I had a very, very bad mouth problem of not bad words and things like that, not profanity. I just had a big mouth. I would jump in and stop other people from saying something and force my opinion.
Okay. You had very strong opinions.

Oh. Very strong opinions. All the time. I’d be no if, ands or buts. I have very strong opinions. And that was my problem. My opinions were always strong, but I was always right. Now I mean no matter how I look at it over all the years, if I practiced what I preached all the time it would be wonderful. But I didn’t always practice what I preached. But believe me, I have very, very strong opinions.
Well obviously at some point you must have butted heads with people who are much like yourself at the time, who also had strong opinions.

I butted heads with a lot of them. And the reason why I’m still here today is that I didn’t know how strong my opinions were, or how much I didn’t know. My naïveness is why I’m alive today, and here. I mean yeah I have strong opinions but I was very, very naïve in my bad parts, or the negative parts. I mean I was like I didn’t mean any harm in what I was saying, but I’m telling you that what you’re talking about, music wise, that’s what it © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
should have been. And my strongest opinion was always in the music and the music business.
And you carry a lot of — as a drummer — you carry a lot of weight as to how things can end up.
Yes.

And the times when you were let’s say butting heads with people, was it often times about the role of the drums and what you think you should play and what the leader or whoever, the singer, whatever — was that sometimes the conflict?
Very seldom.
No kidding.

No. The conflict was where the music was going. How the music was being played. The audience that you’re playing the music to, the concept of what the music was, I was so into the business world that sometimes I lost sight of what I was doing. But I never lost sight of where I thought the music should be and how to make hit records. Because I was with the buying public, I still bought records, I still liked the stars. I was able to pick out the hits because I enjoyed the music. So I had what most people called an insight. Because I listened to everybody. I listened to what people had to say. And then I’d make my opinions about it. But I also made it work musically and commercially. I was taught how to be a commercial salesperson early in life. Now I didn’t know that that wasn’t the way everybody else was doing things. You had a lot of people who just strictly was about the music. This is technically right. Okay. Fine. Yeah. I know that that note, you can play anything. If it sounds good it ain’t wrong. And I mean I was taught that early. And people said no, no, no, no. Sometimes it’s all about the voicing. It’s all about how to make these chords go together and these notes. I said yeah, that’s all good and fine. But does it feel good? Does it sound good? All right the bass player made a mistake. That didn’t stop the record from being good. So you want to be perfect? Is that what you’re saying? And I would be the first one to answer I’m sorry. I can give you a hundred records where there is a mistake, it’s a hit record. So I was never super, super technical. All my life I was told that the music should feel good and should sound good, and it should be good. And that was my thing of how I was brought up. If you can’t tap your foot, something is wrong. If you can’t snap your fingers, something is wrong. If you can’t move your body, something is wrong. And that to me, nothing technical about that. That is all about the love of the music. That is all about the love of the song and it’s about things moving.
It sounds like you had the instincts to be a producer and not just a drummer.

Exactly. And that’s what I was doing and I didn’t know it. And that’s where my mouth got me into trouble. And that’s why I’m talking about being a big mouth. I will be the first one to jump up and tell the arranger and the producer and the writer that you’re © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

wrong. And the part that hurts the most is that I was always right. They did not like it and I can’t blame them. I mean it took me years to understand that, but the point was was that I just had this instinct. And I had it all my life, to make things work. Just make it work. Always thinking about making it work. Putting things together. I could always put things together. I could always put people together. I could always put places together. I could always. I mean I was a natural leader. But I was a great follower. And that’s what you have to be. That’s what I was taught. In order to be a good leader, you must be a great follower. Because unless you let the people know where you’re going or where they’re going, they’re not going to follow you, for you to be a leader. You have to learn something about being a follower. So I had great teachers, and they showed me all those things as I was coming along. So I knew that I was a great follower. I didn’t know I was a great leader. That took a long time for me to know and to understand that. And then of course my ego got in the way in the early parts of my life in the twenties. Because all of a sudden I’m doing all of this work and recording, and people are coming to me and wanting me to be on the date. And I always spoke up. I’ve never not spoken. Oh no. And one of the people that we talked about earlier, Bucky Pizzarelli, he was one of the first ones. He would sit over there and look at me and he’d say “go on, Purdie, go on, Purdie.” And we’d just groove. We instantly hit it off, the first time that we were doing demos.
Rock & roll type demos? R&B things?

Yes, yes. We were doing that. And he was with that guitar and his body, you know his head, shoulders was happening. It wasn’t all about his body and, but the foot was going. But it was just here. Woo. And that hand. I didn’t have to look at his hand, I could see it. I could feel it. I could close my eyes and see him playing on the parts. Because I knew music. I didn’t have any problem there. But woo, man, hit me deep, go right to the soul no matter what he played. And rhythm was the first thing that he would play, no matter what kind of melody that anybody wanted, he played rhythm first and then sneaked the melody in. But it was something else. I mean that to me is how you put folks together. You lock folks in. Guitar, bass, piano. The drummer — if he’s got the bass player, which is of course for the drummer is number one, the bass player is number one — then he has to make a choice between guitar and piano as number two. You don’t know which one is going to be number two until you play.
Like Bucky.

Yeah. And the thing is is that Bucky’s on the date, Bucky becomes number two ninety- nine percent of the time. I don’t care who’s on the piano. When Hank Jones was on the piano I mean there’s nobody can be any finer than him playing the piano and playing chords or playing rhythm or playing melody. But when Bucky and the two of them together I automatically lock in to Bucky with the bass player. And sometimes I ignored © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

the bass player if he wasn’t strong enough because Bucky could carry it. But we always had good strong bass players around. So I mean I really learned about the music itself, of the feel. Yes I was never super, super technical. But when I had to be you talk music. You talk music and you talk shop, whatever it is, I could be on both sides of the fence. That’s when I started to learn about what it meant to be a producer. A producer listens. You don’t go in and say okay this is it, this is what we’re going to do and you play this and you play that. Ah no, no, no. A good producer walks in and says, “Okay let’s see what we got.” Automatically. Let the rhythm section take you on a journey and find out if this is where you want to go. It really is that simple.
Is it better for a producer not to be one of the players?
Doesn’t matter.
Doesn’t matter?

It doesn’t matter. The point is that a good producer is something that — he hears everything and only speaks when he needs to, and takes control when he has to. So he doesn’t have to worry about bending the rules or it gets out of hand with Bucky saying one thing, George Duvivier saying something else and Bernard Purdie saying something else. No. If we’re not locked in it’s his job to stop it. Let’s try it a different way. If he happens to be a player also, he knows. He is supposed to know what’s going to work and what’s going to work for him and lock in to make this music happen. That’s his job. Number one job.

And normally a producer will have — or maybe you can correct me if I’m wrong — but would a producer have been the person responsible for having those let’s say four individuals in that rhythm section there? Because he anticipates that they’re going to work well together?

Exactly. Because they’re in tune with one another. He’s got to look at who’s going to be in tune with one another. Now as big as my mouth, yes I know I have the biggest mouth going, the one thing that I never stopped doing is locking in to the rhythm section. I don’t care which one I had, I don’t care which kind of groove it was, because for me, as I was taught, music is music. Music is color. Music is sound. Music is all these things. But you’ve got to know what idiom that you’re playing in. Jazz. Blues. Rock. R&B. Funk. Latin. It doesn’t matter. You need to be able to play in all of them. And that means being able to read the notes. But in reading the notes you interpret the notes. That’s what reading is to me. That’s how I learned and that’s what my teacher did. Interpreting the music, the notes.

Some of the students that may watch this may have no idea what a record session is actually like. Is it possible for you to just describe it from that first phone call that you get © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
to show up at this particular date, and what that process is like? I know you’ve done so many in so many fields, but what is a typical recording session like?

Okay. In order to do this you really need to know who the producer is. The producer himself or herself, whichever, it’s the one person who knows what the end result is supposed to sound like. Not the arranger. The arranger only gets a certain amount. But it’s the producer who is out with the artist that’s with the writer that formulates what the song is going to be about. Not what it’s going to be like, what it’s going to be about first. So you have to have that the first thing. Then after you this then you go into a rehearsal. Go to where there’s a keyboard or guitar or something and find out what the hook is. The hook is going to suggest who you’re going to have in the band. Oh yeah. Because it’s the hook that’s going to be part of the sound and that sound can be a guitar sound, it can be a piano, it can be a synthesizer, it can be just a sound, a harmonica, it could be a vocal sound, it’s a hook that’s going to grab you, that’s going to make folks want to like and to listen and to play this song over and over and over again. That’s first. And then he goes to call the people that he wants on the session. Now years and years ago, fifties and sixties, you had everybody in the studio at once. So that meant that not only did the producer kind of know, but the arranger now kind of knows what this is going to be like in the end, because of all this music that’s being written out. Well hit records were not made easy at that time because hit records at that time, when you had everybody in, could easily be re- written on the recording date. That’s what happened. Something happened within the rhythm section. Ninety-five percent of the time something happened within the rhythm section which meant guitar, bass, drums, piano. And then coming back and going back where the sixties were you usually had only one drummer, one bass player, but you had three guitar players, one keyboard, maybe two, it varied. Then you have horns, strings, background singers.
Which usually came later? Or were they—

Oh no. This was all done at the same time. This was all done because we’re now dealing with two and four track. Two track and four track. But that’s — you know you’re dealing with the early stages, the stuff that none of the young people today would know or understand because they didn’t have to do it that way. They’ve never known anything like that. So going that way, what happened is that something happened within the rhythm section or a sound happened while you were in there. Now remember now, you already have this hook that you’re looking at, at what you think is going to be the selling point. And that hook has to be now done and laid out. So that hook is going to be in. Now whether that hook is a two bar phrase, a four bar interlude or something that you’re going to back to, back and forth within the song, we don’t know. Nobody knows. But that is what they are selling. That’s their selling point for the song. So you get into the studio, © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

you’ve got this rhythm section going and you start to create this sound. Something happens. Now you’ve got these three guitars. One is playing the backbeat (scats) and you’ve got rhythm (scats) and then you’ve got the other one might be a twang, it might be a thing with Vinnie Bell sound, water sound or a fish or a tree, a whistle. He had all kinds of little sound effects that he did. And this started to become part of the sound to go with the hook of what is happening, the thing that’s going to be repeated over and over and over again. Well that’s how things start to happen. Now for me, I was one of the lucky people. When I was coming along I never believed that the drummer had to be in the background. The drummer did not have to be in the background. Now Gene Krupa helped us. Gene Krupa was one of the first persons to bring us out front so people could see the drums. So I always felt that way because that’s how I was taught when I was coming along. Yes I was taught to play, keep my time. But I was also trying to make the drums outstanding, to be remembered. And that’s how things got with me, which is also why I had some problems with some of the music that was going down, and I was calling it old fashioned. At that particular time people like Bucky and Vinnie Bell and other folks, Bob Bushnell who actually played the Fender bass not the upright, just the upright sound, was coming into play. And it happened to come into what I liked, the kind of things that I did and something that I heard. So it was like wow, this is phenomenal. I’m not the only one that’s hearing things. New thing. Different things. You don’t have to play [scats]. You can play [scats] play it straight. Or you can play [scats] and really play it straight and come out with something that was a little bit different than [scats]. So ooh, I liked this. But still remembering what we were in there for, from what the producer wanted, the sound that the producer wanted to make this thing happen. I said okay, okay, all right, let’s go, let’s go with this. We tried something and the producer, you see the people, the horn players and the string players, they got lines and stuff that’s going on that was happening and then we would ask, well mainly I would ask, if the string players and the horn players don’t play for a minute. Give us five minutes to see if this rhythm is going to fit and maybe, just maybe the arranger might change the rhythm of what he wrote. Still get his figures, but change the rhythm slightly to make it go different and with a dotted feel. Well that was me a lot. That was part of my mouth situation. Well they would give us five minutes. We’d never get more than that, because time is money. We would try some of these things and sure enough these kind of things would happen. Your body started doing this and the arranger, especially if he’s a smart one and really good one, if he starts, he says okay — so you don’t want to go with the dotteds — okay — let’s kind of play this a little bit more straight you know. But he could tell the musicians how to play what he wanted. It was his job. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
So you’re talking about transitioning the music really from more of a swing thing into straight eighth notes.
Yeah.
Can you — this might be a hard question — but can you remember any particular sessions, particular songs where this kind of thing happened?
Sure. Mickey and Sylvia.
Oh. “Love is Strange.”

“Love is Strange.” Yeah. See their first record, the first one that they did in the early fifties was mostly all swing. But it was re-recorded in ’60, ’61. I re-recorded it and brought it with a different sound. Almost straight. But if you hear the record that’s been played all these years, for the last forty years, it’s been their record of the straight time. Not the one that was the shuffle, but more of the straight time. Strings and all. The sound that they had with her moaning and doing two or three different sounds, having the background singers just follow her and not do things on their own. It made all the difference in the world. And that’s the one that’s been played for over forty years, that particular record. So I’ve been very pleased about things like that. “Just One Look,” was my biggest record.
Doris Troy?
Yeah.
I love that record.

It was a straight, you know? I mean we had no strings and horns and stuff like that. We had background singers. And I came in because they couldn’t find another drummer. They went around looking. This was a demo.
I see.

But those are the way things were happening and they were going on. So I got a chance to speak about what I was doing, what I would like to do and that was happening. And they allowed me to do it. So with all those years of running off at the mouth and all of a sudden records becoming hits, I got a reputation. So people gave me the benefit of the doubt of things that I was doing. I was doing something different. Yes he’s got a big mouth, but was making hit records.
So we could put up with it.

We’d put up with it. When the date was over it was over. They didn’t have to deal with me. They weren’t going home with me. They knew this. I mean it was a business to them. But I didn’t know. I didn’t know that I was even alienating people. I mean I was even doing that. Because yeah I got a little arrogant with it after a while. But my arrogance was not like I didn’t know what I was talking about. I was just happy. I was just a kid. I’m coming from nothing to coming to big time. So that’s what my arrogance — when it © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
really happened to hit me, I started to make some money. I mean I was coming home from that $125 a week that I made for all of my work that I was doing, to making $125 a day.
This was —
In the sixties.
In the sixties. So you would make how much for like a demo session or something?
$10 a side.
$10 a side. And how long would that usually take to do one of those?
You did it — an hour.
These are in studios in New York City.
Yeah. And before you knew it I was walking home, like I said, with a hundred dollars, a hundred fifty dollars a day, going home. You know, not a week. And that was big money to me.
What kind, how did the session change so that it became that $150 a night. Were these now record label sessions?

Well the record label sessions were $42.50 for three hours. So if you did two or three sessions during the course of a day, that’s $150 almost $150, because also they were supposed to pay health & welfare and pension. Well you find out much, much later in life that they weren’t.
Oh boy.
Yeah. Well that’s what I’m fighting now so, but it’s going to be okay, it’s going to be okay. It’s all in my favor now. But we even have documentation now.
But if one of these sessions turned out a hit record, the guys in the band did not get more money.

No. We never got more money. We got paid for what we did. And that’s why I thought and every time I would speak up — I was always right when I spoke up, I didn’t just jump up and say no let’s do it this way. I listened to everybody. I listened to everything that went down. And if it wasn’t happening then I’d have something to say. And they did listen to me, the producer, the arranger, the writers, the artists. They did listen. The musicians resented it because well most of the time I didn’t do it right. I really didn’t.
Your delivery of your —
I had no delivery. I am sorry, I had no delivery. It was bad. It was really, really bad. I’d stop guys, no, no man, no it’s wrong.
Okay. Yeah, I can see.
I’m sorry. Then I’m saying I’m sorry, but no man it’s not like that.
It must have hit you, like your musical barometer just something would strike you to be so wrong that you just couldn’t resist. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

And he’s not you.

Exactly. You want Steve, you call him. I’ll be glad to call him for you. But you know when I was coming along I didn’t know that that’s the way it was. You had to play like somebody else in order to do that. Well I didn’t. I played me. But I played and did the job. Now I was fortunate enough to have enough in me to do the job plus. That’s what I’ve done all my life. Do the job plus stick a little bit of me in. And that’s how I’ve done over all these years. I’m going to go in and I’m going to do the job. I’m going to play the music and then I’m going to add a touch of Purdie. Now I thought that’s what you called me for. And after all these years I’m still doing the same thing. I’m still doing the job. But I thought you wanted a little bit of me. And that’s how I do it. So if that means that I’m still arrogant, fine, I’m still arrogant. The point is that I’m there to do the job. I will always love Aretha, the Rolling Stones, Hall & Oates, Steely Dan. I’m always going to love them — B.B. King — like a father to me. The point is is that they called me to do a © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-

job and I said yes I can do it. That’s what I’m going to do. But I get along with everybody and no matter who it is. Cissy, Whitney, it doesn’t matter. That to me is part of life. That’s why I’m in the position that I’m in, that’s why I like everybody, that’s why I can talk about everybody. But I always have something positive to say. Now I could go and I could have made a million dollars instead if I’d have talked about all the bad things about Aretha while I was there. For what? Then I’d never work.
You wouldn’t feel good about yourself either.
Not only that but nobody would hire me to play.
Yeah.
I says no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. Money? I can still earn a good living. So no, no, no. Can’t go that route.

Well listen you’ve been called and you are the world’s most recorded drummer. If we could assemble a rhythm section of the world’s most recorded individual people, who would be playing with you? Do you suppose Milt Hinton would be there?

Well yeah, yeah. Ooh. Wow. Yes Milt Hinton would be. He would definitely be. And then you have folks like people that they forgot about. Bob Bushnell. Bob Bushnell was the first to crack from the upright bass to the Fender. Yeah. Ooh. He did it. And he was the first to do it for ten years. He was doing it almost ten years before it really became popular. So and then you’ve got Bucky Pizzarelli on guitar, you’ve got Eric Gale, I put them all in the same category. Piano, Hank Jones. Jorge Dalto, Richard Tee. I mean, and Paul Griffin.
Oh yeah, I forgot about him.

Well I did so many dates and things with each one of them and Paul Griffin of course we were together with Steely Dan. Larry Carlton, Paul Griffin, Chuck Rainey. I mean you’re talking about the cream of the crop of musicians who could play anything but played what was necessary for what was asked of them at the time. See that’s the beauty. That to me is what it’s about. That’s why I can go anyplace anywhere in the world and play with anybody. Because I know the rhythms. It’s that simple. And you’ve just got to play the right rhythms with what folks want.
It sounds simple. It takes talent that’s for sure.

Well it takes talent but you have to work at what you’re doing for a lot of years. When you work at it and do what needs to be done it works. It definitely works. And it is not a problem for it not — to happen. But you’ve got to know your craft. And that’s all it is. You learn your craft first and then you do it afterwards.
Well just to wrap up here, do you want to tell me how your nickname came about?
When I first came to New York people could not pronounce my last name. They were calling me Bernard Pretty. And after six months the Bernard got dropped and it was © Fillius Jazz Archive -24-

Purdie, hey Pretty Purdie. Pretty Purdie come here. And it was that kind of thing. In the beginning I took it wrong. But after a while it just made sense. It was a good rhyme. There was a good rhythm. It was a good feel. And I liked it, I mean I really and truly liked it. So it was given to me in 1961. I mean I’ve had it since then. And it was something that layed nicely. And like I said when I finally was able to get my name back it was close to the eighties. It was like I started like 1977. I want my name back. Bernard is my name. And people said well we know you as Pretty Purdie. I said yeah, it’s Bernard Pretty Purdie. And they said oh, okay, that’s fine, as long as you keep the Pretty in because that’s what we’re selling. And it was a selling point. So it was cool. So like I said when I first came they couldn’t pronounce my last name and it was Bernard Pretty. And then Pretty Purdie. Like that. Catchy. Or some people would just say hey Pretty. And I mean you know that that’s somebody who really didn’t know me and somebody was trying. Because somebody that knew me would say Purdie, would call me by my last name. So after a while everything was fine and then late eighties and nineties it was just Bernard Purdie. I didn’t have to worry one way or the other, but I decided to keep it because there were people who still knew me as Pretty Purdie. So I said well it’s there, it’s now permanent, it’s Bernard “Pretty” Purdie. And that’s why I use it, the whole thing.
Well I want to tell you it’s been a real privilege to talk to you today, and I have enjoyed it immensely.
My pleasure.
I want to wish you the best on your book.
Oh I’m so happy. I really am. It’s nice.
Well thanks for your time today.
Thank you. My plasma as they say. Well that’s what I say. I still like that.
Sounds good.
It is. It’s very good. © Fillius Jazz Archive -25-

segments.title: Opening and copyright notice
segments.summary: Copyright statement, biographical note and Monk Rowe's introduction.

segments.title: Deciding to be a drummer; first teacher in Elkton
segments.summary: Purdie says he chose music as a baby, played tin pots at three and got a toy set at six. His teacher was the Elkton school band drummer, whom he did not want to emulate as a teacher.

segments.title: Being wrong, arrogance and remembering for his book
segments.summary: Purdie admits being wrong about teaching, reflects on arrogance, truth and memory, and how writing his biography brings back good and painful things.

segments.title: Friends versus associates; power over money
segments.summary: He lost friends who turned out to be associates, says most conflicts were about power rather than money, and credits good teachers.

segments.title: Leonard Heywood, his mentor
segments.summary: Leonard Heywood was his first drum teacher, band director and mentor; he left for Arizona and Purdie wants to dedicate his book to him.

segments.title: Many teachers and his big mouth
segments.summary: Many teachers helped him; he learned to do the job and have fun, but had a big mouth and very strong opinions that made him butt heads.

segments.title: Conflict over where the music was going; feel over technique
segments.summary: His conflicts were about direction of the music, not drums; he picked hits, was taught commercial sense, and valued feel over technical perfection. Rowe says he had a producer's instincts.

segments.title: Leader and follower; locking in with Bucky Pizzarelli
segments.summary: Purdie describes being a natural leader and follower, early demo work, and how he locked in with guitarist Bucky Pizzarelli and the bass player.

segments.title: What a good producer does
segments.summary: A good producer listens, lets the rhythm section lead and picks players who are in tune with each other; Purdie says he always locked in with the rhythm section.

segments.title: Describing a typical recording session
segments.summary: Purdie explains how the producer, the hook, rehearsal and calling players shape a session, with everyone recorded together on two and four track.

segments.title: Rhythm section changing the arrangement; moving to straight time
segments.summary: Purdie describes multiple guitarists such as Vinnie Bell, the drummer out front like Gene Krupa, and asking the arranger for five minutes to alter rhythms toward straight eighths.

segments.title: Mickey and Sylvia and Doris Troy; his reputation
segments.summary: He recalls re-recording Mickey and Sylvia's Love Is Strange in straight time and Doris Troy's Just One Look, and says hits earned him tolerance despite his mouth.

segments.chapter: Money and sessions in the sixties
segments.title: Pay for demos and sessions; unpaid pension
segments.summary: He went from $125 a week to $125 a day, $10 a side for demos, $42.50 for three-hour sessions, and unpaid health, pension and no hit bonuses.

segments.chapter: Money and sessions in the sixties
segments.title: Speaking up on dates and overtime
segments.summary: He explains how his face and mouth betrayed him, how he sometimes caused overtime, and the camaraderie of rhythm sections versus horn and string players.

segments.title: Building rhythms around the singer; Aretha Franklin dates
segments.summary: Without horns and strings present, Purdie built rhythms and counterrhythms around the singer's melody, citing Aretha Franklin hits.

segments.chapter: Money and sessions in the sixties
segments.title: Ernie Royal and consequences of his hollering
segments.summary: He used to holler at trumpeter Ernie Royal about wrong notes; some arrangers resented it but kept calling him as he was often contractor.

segments.title: Favorite sidemen on dates
segments.summary: He names tenor players King Curtis, Sam Taylor, David Newman and guitarists Mickey Baker, Eric Gale and others, and contrasts rhythm sections with horn players who play what is on the page.

segments.title: The book, discography and the internet
segments.summary: His book will include a discography of 1200-2000 records, assembled with Ed Dennis; he comments on errors on the internet.

segments.title: Identifying To Be Free versions on playback
segments.summary: Rowe plays a tune and Purdie identifies it as To Be Free, which he played on in four hit versions, including Nina Simone in 1964.

segments.title: Childhood listening and country music; playing simply
segments.summary: He heard gospel, country, blues and western, loves Floyd Cramer and Ray Charles as country, and learned to play simply and groove.

segments.title: His CD, arrogance mellowed, getting it right
segments.summary: Purdie describes his CD showing ten styles, says he has mellowed, and recalls producers paying overtime to get a take right.

segments.title: Tape change; greed, missing melodies and rap hurting the industry
segments.summary: After a tape change, Purdie says greed, songs without melodies and rap saturation damaged the music industry and shrank profits.

segments.title: Reissues, late audit payment and lawyers running labels
segments.summary: Reissues earned labels money; Purdie got paid in 1994 for 1972 Prestige records after demanding an audit, and criticizes lawyers running companies.

segments.title: Technology, blank media and surviving as a small label
segments.summary: Purdie says big companies profit from blanks and control, while he survives on small sales of his own label.

segments.title: Working with Aretha Franklin and Steely Dan
segments.summary: He loved Aretha but found her personal side hard, found Steely Dan demanding but fine, and says he does the job and leaves.

segments.title: Doing the job plus a touch of Purdie; refusing to bad-mouth
segments.summary: He recalls telling Barry Manilow he is not Steve Gadd, lists artists he loves and refuses to talk badly about Aretha.

segments.title: Dream rhythm section of the most recorded players
segments.summary: Asked for an ideal rhythm section, he names Milt Hinton, Bob Bushnell, Bucky Pizzarelli, Eric Gale, Hank Jones, Richard Tee and Paul Griffin.

segments.title: How he became Pretty Purdie
segments.summary: New Yorkers could not pronounce his name and called him Bernard Pretty, then Pretty Purdie in 1961; he later kept it as a selling point.

segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Rowe thanks Purdie and wishes him well on his book.
